No team, no funding, no meeting rooms. Just one person, one system, and a path that keeps compounding. These are my one-person company field notes.
Can one person really run this?
The questions I get most in DMs — and the things I was most worried about at the start.
Can one person really run a company?

Yes — as long as you only do what only you can do. Product definition, pricing and key judgement stay with you; repetition, follow-ups, email and common questions go to systems and tools. The limit of a company isn't headcount, it's whether you've turned the process into something that can run again.
What if nobody buys at the start?

Sell before you build. Write one paragraph that says who you help, what you solve, what you deliver and what it costs, then send it to 20 people who might have that problem. If someone pays, the need is real. If nobody replies, the writing isn't specific enough. This step needs no product and no company.
When should I register a company?

After the first payment that needs an invoice. Before that, all you need is a contract and a way to get paid. The most expensive part of a one-person company isn't the registration fee — it's stuffing yourself into an org structure you have to maintain.
How do support and after-sales work alone?
the third time I'm asked the same question, it goes into the system.

People with a clear, deliverable skill — developers, designers, consultants, writers. Not for people still looking for direction. A company of one doesn't amplify effort; it amplifies the scarcity you already have.
Year 3 · still a team of one
From one person to one company.
Six steps, from my first client project to automated delivery. Every one of them is doable alone.
Spend a week writing down who you help, what you solve, and what you get in return. If you can't write it, don't register the company yet.
Delivering by hand is fine. Get paid once — what you're validating isn't the product, it's that the need is real.
Turn the repeatable parts of the service into templates, packages or a subscription. Price once, deliver forever.
Forms, payments, delivery, invoices and support replies all go to the toolchain. The goal is zero manual handoffs.
Publish every mistake as a note. Distribution needs no budget, only consistency and honesty.
Watch three numbers a month — revenue, gross margin, and the share of time the system absorbs. Everything else can be deleted.
Year 3 — what the company really looks like.
No launch events, no hockey-stick chart. Just the few numbers that keep moving when one person runs the whole thing.
A company of one runs on leverage, not effort.
One person can't do everything, so picking the right leverage comes first. These six rules are how I cut scope and make decisions every day.
Capital, code, content and AI — four forms of leverage nobody needs permission to use. For every task, ask whether a system could run it again.
Find one paying customer before you find a name. The company is an outcome, not a starting point.
Cash-flow positive from the first invoice. Without funding, profit is the only safety net a solo company has.
Anything done three times becomes a checklist, a script or a template. Spend your hours only on judgement that can't be automated.
Turn the process into content. Readers are the best customer research, hiring channel and co-founder filter you'll ever have.
Capacity comes from consistency, not heroic sprints. Four focused hours a day beats three sleepless weeks.
